extracted.intended_audience: literate general public (readers of The Spectator; early 18th‑century readers interested in manners, morals, and social satire)
extracted.subtask_description: A satirical/moral essay addressing social behaviour, fashions, education, and the relations between sexes; offers prescriptive norms for conduct, upbringing, and public taste. Useful as guidance for composing or judging essays on manners and public morals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid sweeping generalizations about groups
rubrics_metrics.description: “general Charges against Bodies of Men is the Fault I am writing against.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not attribute villainy or demonize whole parties, nations, or classes; the essay gives examples (e.g., the English thought proud, disbelief that great genius could spring from Ireland or Lapland) to show the absurdity of such wholesale charges.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not hold irrational contempt for foreign customs
rubrics_metrics.description: “our common People, and most who have not travelled, have an irrational Contempt for the Language, Dress, Customs, and even the Shape and Minds of other Nations.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Encourage travel and exposure to other cultures as an antidote to parochial scorn; avoid treating national character as a fixed moral indictment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Educators should instill reverence without inflating vanity
rubrics_metrics.description: “It is highly proper to instill such a Reverence of the governing Persons, and Concern for the Honour of the Place, as may spur the growing Members to worthy Pursuits and honest Emulation: But to swell young Minds with vain Thoughts of the Dignity of their own Brotherhood, by debasing and villifying all others, doth them a real Injury.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Teach respect for institutions to motivate effort, but avoid promoting a sense of superiority that leads to laziness, insolence, or contempt for others.

rubrics_metrics.name: Expose youth to diverse exemplars (not just celebrated insiders)
rubrics_metrics.description: “I should think it a surer as well as more generous Method, to set before the Eyes of Youth such Persons as have made a noble Progress in Fraternities less talk'd of; which seems tacitly to reproach their Sloth...”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Present a broad set of role models (including lesser‑known but deserving figures) so young people avoid servile imitation of a few admired men and instead develop independent, generous ambition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Show compassion and assistance for those with lesser talents
rubrics_metrics.description: “Those who are deficient deserve our Compassion, and have a Title to our Assistance.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize variation in talents and educations; encourage support rather than ridicule or exclusion of those less gifted.

rubrics_metrics.name: Discourage servile imitation and affectation
rubrics_metrics.description: “These Copiers of Men, like those of Authors or Painters, run into Affectations of some Oddness... which sits ungracefully on the narrow‑soul'd Transcriber.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Warn against slavish copying of admired individuals, which produces awkward affectations rather than genuine excellence; cultivate original improvement instead.

rubrics_metrics.name: Correct vanity early to cultivate kindness and humanity
rubrics_metrics.description: “By such early Corrections of Vanity, while Boys are growing into Men, they will gradually learn not to censure superficially; but imbibe those Principles of general Kindness and Humanity...”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use early moral education to prevent superficial criticism and to foster empathetic, humane dispositions in young people.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid satirical attacks on entire sexes or professions
rubrics_metrics.description: “I always hated Satyrs against Woman, and Satyrs against Man; I am apt to suspect a Stranger who laughs at the Religion of _The Faculty_; My Spleen rises at a dull Rogue, who is severe upon Mayors and Aldermen;”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Refrain from broad satirical denunciations aimed at whole categories (women, men, officials, professions); prefer measured, targeted critique over wholesale mockery.

rubrics_metrics.name: Maintain a partition between the sexes (discourage cross‑dressing as immodest)
rubrics_metrics.description: “I think it however absolutely necessary to keep up the Partition between the two Sexes, and to take Notice of the smallest Encroachments which the one makes upon the other.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Defend social distinctions of gender dress and behaviour as important to modesty and social order; note and correct small encroachments gently.

rubrics_metrics.name: Address female extravagance with tenderness and gentle methods
rubrics_metrics.description: “For my part, I am for treating the Sex with greater Tenderness, and have all along made use of the most gentle Methods to bring them off from any little Extravagance into which they are sometimes unwarily fallen...”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When correcting fashions or perceived excesses (here, in women), prefer soft persuasion and kindly correction rather than scolding or harsh public censure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treat singularity in dress as likely intentional and scrutinize motive
rubrics_metrics.description: “When I see them singular in any Part of their Dress, I conclude it is not without some Evil Intention; and therefore question not but the Design of this strange Fashion is to smite more effectually their Male Beholders.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be wary of deliberate deviations from convention in dress; consider whether the aim is to attract or to offend, and assess accordingly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mutual regard between sexes improves each
rubrics_metrics.description: “The mutual Regard between the two Sexes tends to the Improvement of each of them... Man would not only be unhappy, but a rude unfinished Creature, were he conversant with none but those of his own Make.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Promote interaction between sexes as refining and civilizing: men gain polish, women gain grace; isolation of either sex leads to degeneration of manners.

rubrics_metrics.name: Criticize political or social factionalism based on trivial fashion markers
rubrics_metrics.description: “The Invention of Marks and Devices to distinguish Parties, is owing to the _Beaux_ and _Belles_... Hats moulded into different Cocks and Pinches... These are the Standard‑Bearers in our contending Armies...”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Warn against allowing trivial sartorial signs (hats, patches, head‑dress) to become the basis for political or social enmity; such markers produce superficial factionalism.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer gallantry and honorable motives in martial combats over mere brutality
rubrics_metrics.description: In discussing public trials of skill and combats: lament that modern fights retain barbarity but have lost the amorous gallantry of earlier times.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When depicting or organizing public contests (duels, trials of skill), emphasize gallant and honorable intent (for a lady, for reputation) rather than sheer vicious spectacle; the essay contrasts spectacle‑seeking crowds with more noble motivations.
